To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DNA plasmid vectors are safe and suitable for human use.

repeated-dose toxicological safety studies in animals of DNA plasmids expressing different genes, using different plasmid back bones, have not identified any intrinsic toxicities or immunotoxicities of these DNA plasmid constructs.
repeated-dose toxicities of our DNA plasmids are confined to the site of injection and seem reversible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel vaccine strategies for the prevention of infectious diseases.
developing and evaluating novel DNA vaccines against infectious agents that are of high priority for public health.

the development of safe and effective vaccines against a variety of infectious diseases, including HIV-1/AIDS, Severe Acutely Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), Ebola virus, West Nile (WN) virus, and others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the repeated-dose safety evaluation of DNA vaccine constructs against HIV-1 and Ebola virus, as well as the plasmid cytokines adjuvant IL-2/Ig, is similar despite differing promoters, plasmid back-bones, or gene-inserts.
DNA vaccines have been shown to be safe in animal models, and that the safety profile of DNA vaccines is similar across the various indications and plasmid back bone designs.
the toxicological safety evaluation of our DNA plasmids is similar regardless of the disease indication, plasmid backbone, or expressed gene-insert.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNA plasmid vaccination can be safely and effectively delivered to humans, with the safety profile of the DNA plasmid itself not differing significantly between different disease indications.
the safety of DNA plasmids as vaccines can be predicted from the biodistribution data.
the safety profile for these DNA plasmid-based vaccines is very similar, regardless of plasmid backbone or gene-insert.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the toxicology studies we have conducted are not likely to be predictive of any immunotoxicity or intrinsic toxicity of our DNA vaccine candidates, and thus may be unnecessary for these vaccines.
the toxicological safety profile of DNA plasmids is similar, regardless of the disease indication, the plasmid backbone, or the plasmid gene insert.
